newsitem.title: ITALY: ALPINE SKIING-TOMBA SAYS HE IS READY TO RACE.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-TOMBA SAYS HE IS READY TO RACE.

text.p: Alberto Tomba, telling Alpine skiing fans and his World Cup rivals alike that the long wait was over, declared on Monday he was ready to race for the first time this season.

The Italian, sidelined by a heavy fall while training pre-season, told a news conference before Tuesday's slalom in Madonna di Campiglio he was looking forward to skiing against the others again after last racing in March.
However the reigning world slalom champion added he was not convinced they would be quite so eager to see him.
"Here I am. It's been a long time to wait," he said.
To be precise, it has been 281 days since the triple Olympic gold medallist last skied competitively and the sport desperately needs a dose of his personality.
The Italian won on the relatively short Canalone Miramonti piste last year, his first win of what became a triumphant season and also a race run on his 29th birthday.
This year's slalom comes a few days earlier in the calendar -- his birthday is on Thursday -- and Tomba said that he was nowhere near as ready now as he had been before.
He said he had done about a tenth of the training and had targetted Campiglio because it was a shorter and not so demanding piste than some of the other slaloms.
A leg took around 40 seconds to complete last year and "La Bomba" said he would be out of gas for anything much longer. Sunday's giant slalom in Alta Badia looked doubtful.
"I don't want to go to do badly. I'll probably go but just to say 'hi' to the fans," the Bolognese said.

Since March there has been much agonising debate about whether or not Tomba should retire, a decision now shelved until at least after the next world championships in the Italian resort of Sestriere and possibly to the end of the millenium.
"Last season I thought that I would stop. Then a lot of people asked me to carry on," he said.
"I don't know how long I will carry on but I want to prove that at 30 I can still be as good as at 20."
Tomba said he needed to get back into the action as soon as possible because a longer absence would otherwise damage his world ranking and place in the starting lineup.

It is the third men's slalom of the season and the first on European snow, with the others won by in-form Austrian Thomas Sykora in Park City and Norwegian Tom Stiansen, winning his first slalom, in the U.S. resort of Breckenridge.
Sykora leads the world slalom standings with 180 points, ahead of compatriot Thomas Stangassinger on 140.
The course was a little soft on Monday but Tomba, who intends to wear a light cast on his wrist, said he was confident it would harden overnight before the race.

Last year, after a disastrous piece of public relations at Alta Badia -- where he threw a glass trophy and a magnum of champagne at a photographer who had sold nude photos of him -- Tomba's fans rallied round with a cake at Madonna.
Tomba won the race and apologised to the photographer.
The Italian said that this year, faced with a rare race-free day on his birthday, he might just slip off and celebrate quietly with his friends and family in Bologna.
